guides.title: Is Cape Verde Safe? Official Travel Advice, Crime, Sea and Health
guides.summary: The US rates Cape Verde Level 1, with Level 2 advice for Praia; the FCDO publishes precautions for visitors. Watch for petty crime in Praia, Sal and Boa Vista, strong currents, basic medical care and dengue.
guides.html:
Is Cape Verde (officially Cabo Verde) safe to visit? The honest answer is to read what the governments that track it say, and to know the specific risks they name. This guide sets out the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) and US State Department positions as they stand in November 2026, then works through crime, the sea, health, getting between islands, driving and the local laws visitors can break without realising. We add no reassurance or alarm of our own.

What the UK and US governments say

GovernmentCurrent positionDate
UK (FCDO)No advice against travel to any part of Cape Verde; general warning that no travel can be guaranteed safeUpdated 28 July 2026, still current at 16 November 2026
US (State Department)Level 1: Exercise Normal Precautions, due to crime; Praia: Level 2, Exercise Increased CautionIssued 18 December 2025

The State Department's summary says Cabo Verde is generally a safe destination for travelers and that some areas have increased risk. Its full advisory places Praia at Level 2, Exercise Increased Caution, naming petty crime and violent crime including mugging, armed robbery and assault. The FCDO's July 2026 update concerned travelling with medication.

Crime: what happens and where

The FCDO says the crime rate in Cape Verde is generally low, but can include pickpocketing, bag snatching, burglary and muggings, particularly in the capital, Praia, and on the islands of Sal and Boa Vista. It adds that sexual assaults are rare but have been reported.

The FCDO's suggested precautions are practical:

  • leave valuables somewhere secure, such as a hotel safe
  • keep your belongings in sight in bars and restaurants
  • do not carry large amounts of cash or wear expensive jewellery
  • avoid unlit and isolated areas after dark
  • avoid beaches with limited or restricted visibility
  • keep your accommodation's windows and doors locked

In practice that means not leaving a phone on the sand while you swim at Santa Maria beach, walking back along lit streets in Santa Maria or Sal Rei at night, and using a taxi rather than an empty beach path. The FCDO also says there is no recent history of terrorism in Cape Verde, but attacks cannot be ruled out.

The sea: currents, waves and beach flags

The FCDO is direct about the Atlantic here: tides and currents around the islands are very strong, waves can be unpredictable and have a strong undertow. Its advice is to always use beaches where there is a lifeguard on duty, to take care walking close to the water's edge on unsupervised beaches, and to follow lifeguards and the flags:

  • Red: danger, do not go into the water.
  • Yellow: caution, you can walk in the water but you cannot swim.
  • Green: safe to swim.

If you cannot see a lifeguard, treat the beach as one of the unsupervised stretches the FCDO warns about; long, open beaches such as Praia de Santa Mónica on Boa Vista deserve that caution. For water sports such as kitesurfing, surfing or scuba diving, ask a qualified school to assess the conditions before entering. Check the specific beach page before you go: Ponta Preta and Kite Beach on Sal are wind and wave spots, not paddling beaches.

Health risks

The UK's official travel health service, TravelHealthPro (NaTHNaC), and the FCDO name these risks for Cape Verde:

  • Stomach bugs: the FCDO says the UK Health Security Agency has investigated an increase in Shigella sonnei and Salmonella in travellers returning from Cape Verde. Reported cases have decreased, but there is still a risk of gastrointestinal illness. TravelHealthPro reported in February 2026 that most Shigella cases had visited Santa Maria and Boa Vista. The advice is good hand hygiene and food and water precautions.
  • Tap water: we found no specific verdict on Cape Verde's tap water on the FCDO and TravelHealthPro pages read for this guide. They advise care with personal, food and water hygiene. Follow your hotel's guidance and use bottled or treated water if in doubt.
  • Dengue: TravelHealthPro says there is a risk of dengue, spread by mosquitoes that mainly bite in the daytime. The FCDO says the Cape Verde government has raised the civil protection warning level for dengue on Santiago, Fogo and Brava.
  • Zika: TravelHealthPro says there is a risk of Zika, and advises pregnant women to discuss travel with a health professional.
  • Malaria: TravelHealthPro says the WHO declared Cape Verde malaria-free in 2024 and that there is no risk of malaria, while recommending bite avoidance. Its outbreak log also records 16 locally acquired malaria cases in Praia reported as of 21 August 2025. Ask a travel health clinician if you are heading to Praia.
  • Altitude: the FCDO notes altitude sickness is a risk on Fogo, relevant if you are climbing Pico do Fogo.

Use insect repellent by day as well as in the evening, and see a travel health clinic at least 8 weeks before you go, as the FCDO recommends.

Medical care, evacuation and insurance

The FCDO says medical facilities are basic and limited, some medicines are in short supply or unavailable, and medication is only available from pharmacies. The largest hospitals are in Praia on Santiago and in Mindelo on São Vicente, with smaller clinics elsewhere; facilities are particularly limited on Boa Vista. Brava and Santo Antão have no working airports, so medical air evacuation from there is extremely difficult.

Two points follow directly from the FCDO advice:

  • Insurance is essential. The UK Global Health Insurance Card (GHIC) is not accepted in Cape Verde. Your policy should cover local treatment and medical evacuation, and any activities you plan.
  • Quad bikes are a special case. The FCDO calls quad biking an extreme sport that is unlikely to be covered by standard insurance, and says that after a quad bike accident you will highly likely need medical evacuation. Check your cover before booking desert and dune tours on a quad.

Bring enough of any prescribed medicine for the whole trip plus a few days' spare in hand luggage.

Getting between islands: expect disruption

Island hopping is one of the joys of Cape Verde, but the FCDO is clear that sea conditions around the islands can be dangerous and that sea travel to the southern islands of Brava and Fogo in particular can often be disrupted. It advises following local advice before travelling by sea. Air travel has its own weather risk: sandstorms, called bruma seca, can happen between December and February and, when intense, can disrupt flights, especially on Boa Vista. Build spare days into any itinerary that depends on a ferry or domestic flight, and never plan to catch an international flight home on the same day as an inter-island connection. Our island-hopping page and island-hopping guide cover the options.

Weather, earthquakes and volcano country

The FCDO says the rainy season runs from mid-August to mid-October, and torrential rain on some islands can cause flooding and landslides. It also says tremors are felt occasionally, mostly on Brava and Fogo, usually within normal bounds but sometimes dangerous; check with your travel provider before travelling to those islands. For seasons, see the best time to visit Cape Verde and our weather page.

Driving, taxis and buses

  • Licences: the FCDO says a valid UK photocard licence can be used for up to 6 months; paper licence holders need the 1968 International Driving Permit as well. You will be arrested if you are found driving without a licence.
  • Hire vehicles: check that a car, scooter or quad is in good condition and fully insured. Hire firms often want a year of driving experience, a higher minimum age and an IDP.
  • Helmets: wearing a crash helmet on a scooter or quad bike is a legal requirement, and riding without one may invalidate your insurance.
  • Taxis: only use authorised taxis from ranks or called by your hotel. On Sal and Boa Vista, authorised taxis are blue and yellow.
  • Intercity buses: the FCDO says they can be dangerous because of poor driving.

More on transport is on our transportation page.

Laws visitors break by accident

  • Drugs: severe penalties for possessing, using or trafficking, including fines and long prison sentences.
  • No helmet on a scooter or quad: an offence, as above.
  • Driving without a licence: the FCDO says this leads to arrest.
  • Travelling with someone else's child: children aged 17 and under without a parent or guardian need a certified letter of authorisation in Portuguese, or may be refused entry.
  • Pre-registration: the FCDO says that from 1 July 2026, failing to complete pre-registration or show proof means paying double the airport security fee at border control, as of November 2026. See our entry requirements guide.

The FCDO also notes British nationals have had problems buying property in Cape Verde and advises independent legal advice first.

Emergency numbers

ServiceNumber
Ambulance130
Fire131
Police132

These are the numbers the FCDO lists. Save them, your insurer's emergency line and your hotel's number before you go, and see our emergency contacts page.

Choosing where to go

The FCDO names Praia, Sal and Boa Vista for petty crime, Brava and Fogo for sea disruption and tremors, Boa Vista for limited medical facilities and sandstorm flight disruption, and Brava and Santo Antão for difficult evacuation. Use that to plan: for example, hikers on Santo Antão should carry insurance with evacuation cover. Compare islands in which Cape Verde island is best and Sal or Boa Vista.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Cape Verde safe for tourists?

The US State Department rates Cabo Verde Level 1, Exercise Normal Precautions, citing crime (issued 18 December 2025), with Praia at Level 2, Exercise Increased Caution. The UK FCDO does not advise against travel to any part of the country. Both name petty crime, and the FCDO stresses strong sea currents and basic medical care.

Where is crime most common in Cape Verde?

The FCDO names the capital Praia and the islands of Sal and Boa Vista for pickpocketing, bag snatching, burglary and muggings. Use a hotel safe, avoid unlit and isolated areas after dark, avoid secluded beaches and do not carry large amounts of cash.

Is it safe to swim in Cape Verde?

Only with care. The FCDO says tides and currents around the islands are very strong and waves can have a strong undertow. Swim only where a lifeguard is on duty and obey the flags: red means stay out, yellow means wade but do not swim, green means swimming is safe.

Can you drink the tap water in Cape Verde?

We found no specific verdict on Cape Verde's tap water on the UK official health pages read for this guide. They advise care with food and water hygiene, and note cases of Shigella and Salmonella in returning travellers. Follow your hotel's advice and use bottled or treated water if in doubt.

Is there malaria or dengue in Cape Verde?

TravelHealthPro says the WHO declared Cape Verde malaria-free in 2024 and lists no malaria risk, though it also logged locally acquired cases in Praia in 2025. It says there is a risk of dengue and Zika. Avoid mosquito bites day and night.

What are the emergency numbers in Cape Verde?

The FCDO lists 130 for an ambulance, 131 for the fire service and 132 for the police. Medical facilities are basic, so also keep your travel insurer's emergency assistance number to hand.

Are ferries and domestic flights in Cape Verde reliable?

Not always. The FCDO says sea travel to Brava and Fogo in particular can often be disrupted, and sandstorms between December and February can disrupt flights, especially on Boa Vista. Leave spare days and avoid same-day connections to international flights.

Do I need travel insurance for Cape Verde?

Yes. The FCDO says the UK GHIC card is not accepted, care is basic and limited, and evacuation from some islands is extremely difficult. Choose a policy that covers local treatment, medical evacuation and any activities such as quad biking.

guides.duration: Applies to any length of stay

guides.title: Sal or Boa Vista? Which Cape Verde Island to Choose
guides.summary: Sal suits walkers, kitesurfers and people who want a lively town; Boa Vista suits all-inclusive stays, empty beaches and whale season. Here is how they compare point by point.
guides.html:
For most people booking a winter-sun week in Cape Verde (officially Cabo Verde), the real decision is between two islands: Sal and Boa Vista. Both are flat, dry and fringed with pale sand, both have international airports, and both are windy for much of the year. On the ground, though, they suit different people. Sal is compact, busier and built around a walkable town. Boa Vista is bigger, emptier and built around large resorts. Here is the comparison point by point.

Sal or Boa Vista at a glance

FactorSalBoa Vista
Main baseSanta Maria, a walkable resort townResorts along the coast, plus the town of Sal Rei
BeachesOne long town beach plus wind-sport beachesLonger, emptier beaches, some very remote
SwimmingChoose a beach with a lifeguard on dutyVaries a lot by beach; some exposed
Wind sportsKite Beach and Ponta PretaWind sports around Sal Rei
Airport transferCheck transfer to Santa MariaCheck transfer to Sal Rei or resort
WildlifeTurtles in season, lemon sharks all yearThe main turtle island; humpback whales in spring
NightlifeBars and live music in Santa MariaMostly inside the resorts; some in Sal Rei
FlightsCheck routes for your travel datesCheck routes for your travel dates

Beaches and swimming safety

Sal's star is Santa Maria beach, a long curve of white sand running either side of the Santa Maria pier. Choose where to swim according to the lifeguard and the conditions on the day. Further west, Ponta Preta is a surf and kite beach rather than a swimming one, and Kite Beach on the east coast is exactly what the name says.

Boa Vista has more and bigger beaches. Praia de Chaves backs onto dunes, Praia de Santa Mónica on the south coast runs for kilometres, Praia de Estoril is the town beach at Sal Rei, and Praia da Varandinha adds another option. Ponta Sino is on Sal. Space is the reward; the trade-off is that many of these beaches are open to the Atlantic swell.

On both islands, treat the sea with respect. The UK government's travel advice, still current as of 16 November 2026, says tides and currents around the islands are very strong and that waves can be unpredictable with a strong undertow. It advises swimming only where a lifeguard is on duty and following the flags: red means do not go in, yellow means you may walk in the water but not swim, green means it is safe to swim. If you have young children, a resort pool or a lifeguarded section of beach matters more than which island you pick.

Wind

Both islands are windy, especially in the season when the north-east trade winds are common, with December to March recommended for kitesurfing by the tourism institute. That is ideal for kitesurfing and windsurfing, and Sal has schools and spots to consider. On the beach, the same wind blows sand around and cools the afternoon air. A sheltered sunbed matters more than you might expect; ask your hotel how protected its beach and pool area are. Between December and February, dust from the Sahara (the harmattan haze) can dull the sky on both islands, and the UK government notes that intense sandstorms can disrupt air travel, especially on Boa Vista.

Resort life or town life

This is the biggest practical difference. Santa Maria on Sal is a real small town: choose accommodation near the restaurants, bars, pier and beach if you want to walk out each evening. It suits couples and anyone who dislikes staying inside a resort all week.

On Boa Vista, many visitors stay in large all-inclusive resorts spread along the coast, some a long way from anything else. They are self-contained and quiet, which many families want, but stepping out for dinner usually means a taxi. If you would like a town nearby, choose a hotel in or close to Sal Rei, which has a harbour, a square and local restaurants. On both islands the UK government notes that authorised taxis are blue and yellow.

Airport transfers

Sal airport sits near Espargos in the middle of the island, so check your transfer to Santa Maria. Boa Vista airport serves Sal Rei and the resorts, but transfers vary because some hotels are on the far coasts. Check your hotel's distance from the airport before booking if you are arriving late at night with children.

Excursions

Sal's excursions are short and easy to combine into one island tour. The Pedra de Lume salt crater has salt pans inside the crater of an extinct volcano, where you float in the brine. The Buracona blue eye is a sunlight effect in an underwater tunnel beside a natural pool on the west coast. At Shark Bay, juvenile lemon sharks use the shallows of Parda Reef as a nursery all year, and Terra Boa is known for its heat-haze mirage. Snorkelling, scuba diving and sport fishing trips leave from Santa Maria.

Boa Vista's excursions are about scale and emptiness. Desert and dune tours cross the Viana desert, the dunes of the Morro de Areia nature reserve and the rusting Cabo Santa Maria shipwreck on the north coast. Expect long drives on rough tracks; a quad or 4x4 day is a highlight for some and a long bumpy ride for others.

Turtles and whales

Loggerhead turtles nest on both islands. Boa Vista is the main nesting island. Sal has a smaller but monitored nesting population. The nesting season runs from June to October, with hatchlings typically seen from the end of August into early December. The conservation group Project Biodiversity states that watching must be done on certified or government-licensed guided tours, that visiting nesting beaches at night without a guide is prohibited in the season, and that visitors must wear dark clothes, use no lights or phone flash, and never touch a turtle. See turtle watching for the full rules.

Whales tip the balance toward Boa Vista in spring. Humpback whales breed in Cape Verde between February and May, and a study in the Journal of Cetacean Research and Management described the bay off Sal Rei as the single most important winter breeding bay for the species in the eastern North Atlantic. Whale-watching trips run from Boa Vista in season.

Nightlife

Sal wins easily. Santa Maria has beach bars, restaurants with live music and a few late venues, so consider a base near the places you want to visit. Boa Vista's nightlife is mostly inside the resorts, with a handful of bars in Sal Rei. If hearing live music and morna is a priority, either island will give you a taste, and consider Mindelo on São Vicente for a music-focused trip.

Families

Both islands work for families, in different ways. On Boa Vista, check whether your chosen resort has the pool and children's facilities you need. Sal suits families with older children who want to walk into town, try a surfing or kite lesson, and see the sharks at Shark Bay. With toddlers, prioritise a hotel with a sheltered pool and a lifeguarded beach on either island.

Who should pick which

  • Choose Sal if you want a walkable town, a choice of restaurants, kitesurfing or windsurfing, suitable flights for your dates, or a short first trip. The things to do in Sal guide and the Sal 5-day itinerary help you plan.
  • Choose Boa Vista if you want a big all-inclusive resort, emptier beaches, a desert landscape, or whales in spring. See things to do in Boa Vista and the Boa Vista 5-day itinerary.
  • Choose neither if you want mountains, history or a trip focused on cultural sights: read which Cape Verde island is best instead.

Why doing both in one week is hard

On a map the two islands look close, so it is tempting to split a week between them. In practice it is awkward. Check CV Interilhas sailings and CVsky flights for your actual travel dates, as of November 2026. The FCDO warns that sea conditions can be dangerous and sandstorms can disrupt flights. Allow time for packing, transfers and check-in on both sides.

If you want both, give it ten days or more, book the inter-island leg first, and keep a spare day before your flight home. Read island hopping and the island-hopping guide for current options. For most one-week trips, pick one island and enjoy it properly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Sal or Boa Vista better for a first trip to Cape Verde?

Sal, for most people. Check flights and airport transfers for your dates; Santa Maria offers a town base. Boa Vista is the better pick if you specifically want a large all-inclusive resort and very quiet beaches.

Which island has better beaches, Sal or Boa Vista?

Boa Vista's beaches are longer and emptier. Sal's Santa Maria beach offers a town base; calm water should not be assumed. On both, follow the beach flags and swim where a lifeguard is on duty.

Is Boa Vista or Sal windier?

Both are windy, and the tourism institute recommends December to March for kitesurfing. Ask your hotel how sheltered its pool and beach area are if you plan to spend long days lounging.

Can you see turtles on Sal as well as Boa Vista?

Yes. Loggerheads nest on both islands from June to October, though Boa Vista has far more nests. Watch only with a certified guide; going onto nesting beaches at night without one is prohibited in the season.

Can I easily visit Boa Vista on a day trip from Sal?

Not reliably. Check the actual ferry and flight departures before committing to a day trip. Split a longer trip between them or choose one.
guides.bestTime: December to March for kitesurfing; February to May for whales; check the authorised turtle-tour season
guides.duration: One island for 7 days; both only with 10 days or more
guides.budget: Compare package prices and allow a separate budget for meals and excursions

guides.title: Things to Do in Boa Vista, Cape Verde: Dunes, Beaches, Wildlife
guides.summary: Boa Vista is the big, empty, sandy island. This guide groups its beaches, dunes, wreck and wildlife by interest, gives the official watching rules, and flags what the island does not offer.
guides.html:
Boa Vista is one of the emptiest islands in Cape Verde. It is mostly sand and stony plain, ringed by long beaches, with the town of Sal Rei, on the west coast and its international airport, Aristides Pereira International (BVC), a short drive away. Most visitors come for the beaches and the dunes, and that is a fair summary of what this corner of Cabo Verde, to give the country its official name, does best. Below, the island's sights are grouped by interest, with turtle-watching rules and whale-watching guidance and a straight answer on what Boa Vista is not good for.

Beaches

Boa Vista's beaches are long, wide and, away from the resorts, often empty. Four are worth knowing by name.

  • Praia de Chaves: a broad beach backed by dunes south of Sal Rei, with resort hotels at one end and open sand beyond.
  • Praia de Santa Mónica: a very long beach on the south-west coast, quiet and remote once you walk away from the resort stretch.
  • Praia de Estoril: the town beach of Sal Rei, handy for a swim, a drink and the water sports centres.
  • Praia da Varandinha: a rocky, dramatic stretch of coast in the south-west, better for walking and photographs than for a beach day.

Size has a downside: do not assume that a remote beach has a lifeguard, shade or phone reception. The UK government's travel advice warns that tides and currents around the islands are very strong and that waves can have a strong undertow, and tells visitors to use beaches where a lifeguard is on duty. Check that a lifeguard is actually on duty rather than assuming hotel or town beaches are supervised. Treat remote beaches as walks, not swims.

Dunes and desert

The Viana desert (Deserto de Viana) inland from Sal Rei is a field of pale dunes that looks more Saharan than Atlantic. Consider it for desert and dune tours by 4x4, quad or on foot with a guide. Go early or late in the day: the sand is hot by midday and the light is flat.

The dunes of the Morro de Areia nature reserve are a designated Natural Reserve in the country's national network of protected areas. Several of Boa Vista's protected areas are dunes and beaches used by nesting turtles, and Project Biodiversity lists quads and cars on the sand among the activities that destroy dune habitat. If you book a motorised tour, choose one that keeps to tracks, and stay off the dunes on nesting beaches.

Wind is part of the desert experience. The UK advice says sandstorms (bruma seca) can happen between December and February and that, when intense, they can disrupt air travel, especially on Boa Vista. A hazy day is a poor day for dune photographs, so keep your tour date flexible if you can.

The Cabo Santa Maria shipwreck

The rusting hull of the Cabo Santa Maria, a cargo ship that ran aground on the north coast, is one of the island's sights. It sits just off a wide, windswept beach and can be combined with the Viana desert on a northern island tour. The wreck is breaking up: look from the sand, do not climb on it, and do not swim out to it, because the surf and currents along this coast are strong.

The north of the island also holds the Boa Esperança Natural Reserve, another protected area in the national network. Expect rough tracks rather than roads, and consider a guided trip if you are unfamiliar with the route.

Turtle watching

Boa Vista is one of the islands that make Cape Verde globally important for loggerhead turtles. Project Biodiversity notes that the beaches of Sal, Boa Vista and Maio have significant nesting populations and says the archipelago is the world's third-largest loggerhead nesting site. Nesting walks are therefore a summer highlight, and they are tightly regulated.

The charity gives the official observation dates for 2026 as 1 July until the end of September, excluding specific nesting beaches. Under the national turtle watching regulation (Decreto-lei n.º 50/2024), visitors may only use red-light torches, with white light and flash banned; a group of no more than ten visitors approaches each turtle in a line behind the nature guide; and visitors may never be left alone on the beach. Book turtle watching through a guided excursion and do not walk nesting beaches with a torch on your own.

Whale watching

Humpback whales come to Cape Verde's waters to breed and calve, and the waters around Boa Vista are among the best known for sightings. A good-practice guide for nature excursions, validated by the national environment and tourism directorates, says two humpback populations use the islands: the North Atlantic one from February to May and a Southern Hemisphere one from July to October. For a winter or spring holiday, the February to May window is the one that matters.

The same guide sets a watching zone of at least 60 metres from the whales, rising to 100 metres when calves are present, with a limit on total time spent with them. A good whale watching operator will brief you on this before leaving port and will not chase animals for a photograph.

Wind and water sports

Boa Vista offers wind sports around Sal Rei. Kitesurfing and windsurfing schools work from the bay at Sal Rei, where you should ask about the conditions on the day. Experienced riders head for wilder spots with a guide. Surfing depends on swell and calls for advice from a qualified instructor.

Under the water, scuba diving and snorkelling trips leave from Sal Rei and the resorts, and sport fishing boats go out for bigger fish offshore. Check the sea state before booking.

Sal Rei: the town

Sal Rei is small, walkable and a base for seeing everyday Cape Verdean life. Spend an evening around the main square and the streets behind the seafront, where small restaurants serve cachupa, fresh fish, grilled lobster when it is in, and goat's cheese, queijo de cabra, often with papaya jam. Bars sometimes have live music, and a glass of grogue or ponche finishes the night.

Offshore, the islet facing the town is protected as the Monte Ilhéu de Sal-Rei Natural Monument. Other protected sites dot the island, among them the Ponta do Sol Natural Reserve and the Rocha Estância and Monte Santo António natural monuments. A guided island tour is the easiest way to see a few of them.

What Boa Vista is not good for

  • Exploring on your own. Distances are long and much of the island is reached on sand or stony tracks. A guided tour or a driver is usually more practical than a hire car.
  • Nightlife and choice. Outside the all-inclusive resorts and Sal Rei, there is very little. If you want a lively town with lots of restaurants, Santa Maria on Sal is the better base.
  • Hiking, green landscapes and history. Like Sal, Boa Vista is dry and low. For mountains go to Santo Antão or Fogo; for history, Cidade Velha on Santiago.
  • Swimming anywhere. Many of the most beautiful beaches are unsupervised and exposed to strong currents.
  • Turtle walks in winter. Nesting watches are limited by law to the summer season.

For a side-by-side view of the two resort islands, read Sal or Boa Vista, and for a wider look at the country, things to do in Cape Verde.

Practical notes

  • Getting there and away: check CVsky flight availability for your dates, as of November 2026. Our island hopping guide covers the flights and ferry options.
  • Taxis: UK advice says that on Sal and Boa Vista authorised taxis are blue and yellow; use those, or ask your hotel to call one.
  • Safety: the same advice says crime is generally low but mentions pickpocketing, bag snatching and muggings particularly in Praia and on Sal and Boa Vista. See is Cape Verde safe and emergency contacts.
  • Planning: our Boa Vista 5-day itinerary puts these sights in order, the best time to visit Cape Verde covers seasons, and visa and entry requirements covers the pre-arrival registration.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days do you need on Boa Vista?

Four or five days cover a northern tour with the Viana desert and the wreck, a southern beach day at Santa Mónica, an evening in Sal Rei and a boat trip. A week leaves room for kitesurfing lessons or simple rest.

When can you see whales off Boa Vista?

The North Atlantic humpback population is in Cape Verde's waters from February to May, according to a good-practice guide validated by the national environment and tourism directorates. A second, Southern Hemisphere population uses the islands from July to October.

Can you watch turtles nesting on Boa Vista?

Yes, in season and with a guide. The official observation dates for 2026 were 1 July to the end of September, and the national regulation limits groups to ten visitors per turtle, with red light only and no flash photography.

Can you visit the Cabo Santa Maria wreck on your own?

It is possible with a suitable vehicle, but the tracks are rough and the coast is remote, so consider a guided northern tour. Stay on the beach, do not climb on the hull, and do not swim out to it.

Is Boa Vista quieter than Sal?

Yes. It is larger, with Sal Rei as a town base, which suits beach walkers and families in all-inclusive resorts. If you want restaurants and bars within walking distance, Sal is the easier choice.

guides.title: Things to Do in Cape Verde: The Best Experiences by Island
guides.summary: From kitesurfing on Sal and turtles on Boa Vista to Cidade Velha on Santiago, morna in Mindelo, Santo Antão trails and the climb up Pico do Fogo: what to do and which island it is on.
guides.html:
For a beach holiday in Cape Verde (officially Cabo Verde), consider Sal or Boa Vista. The islands also hold a fifteenth-century colonial town, a volcano you can climb, valleys built for walking and a live-music culture that UNESCO recognises. The catch is that each experience sits on a particular island, and moving between islands takes planning. This guide is organised by interest, with the island named for every item, so you can see what is realistic from where you are staying.

Spend lazy days on the beaches

The best beaches are on the flat eastern islands. On Sal, Santa Maria beach is the classic: long, white and facing south, away from the prevailing wind, with the town of Santa Maria right behind it. On Boa Vista, Praia de Santa Mónica and Praia de Chaves run for kilometres with hardly a building in sight, and Praia de Estoril is the easy town beach at Sal Rei.

Elsewhere, Tarrafal beach on Santiago sits in a calm, curved bay, Bitxe Rotxa on Maio is close to empty, and Laginha is Mindelo's town beach. Whichever you choose, the UK government's travel advice warns that tides and currents around the islands are very strong: swim where a lifeguard is on duty and follow the flags. Browse all Cape Verde beaches for more.

Ride the wind and get in the water

Sal is the wind-sports island. The tourism institute recommends December to March for wind sports, which is why Kite Beach on the east coast and Ponta Preta in the south-west fill with riders. Schools on Sal teach kitesurfing and windsurfing from first lessons upward, and when the swell arrives Ponta Preta is also a surfing spot for experienced riders.

Under the water, scuba diving and snorkelling trips leave from Santa Maria and Sal Rei, and sport fishing boats head offshore for big game. On Sal, Shark Bay is a shallow reef flat where juvenile lemon sharks use the water as a nursery all year round; you wade in and watch them circle. Stay calm, keep your hands to yourself and let them come to you.

Watch turtles and whales

Boa Vista is an important loggerhead turtle nesting island in Cape Verde. The nesting season runs from June to October, and hatchlings emerge from August to December. Nesting also happens on Sal, where it is monitored by local conservation teams.

The nesting season is longer than the permitted observation window. As of November 2026, Project Biodiversity gives the 2026 observation dates as 1 July to the end of September, excluding specific nesting beaches. Confirm future dates with a licensed operator. According to the conservation group Project Biodiversity, turtle watching must be done on a certified or government-licensed guided tour, and going onto nesting beaches at night without a guide is prohibited during the season. Wear dark clothes, switch off every light and phone flash, keep no more than ten people behind a nesting female, approach only once she has started laying, and never touch her or block her path to the sea.

In late winter and spring, humpback whales come to breed. The breeding season runs from February to May, and researchers have described the bay off Sal Rei on Boa Vista as the single most important winter breeding bay for humpbacks in the eastern North Atlantic. Book whale watching from Boa Vista between those months for the best chance.

Float in salt and cross the desert

Two islands look more like the Sahara than the Atlantic. On Sal, the Pedra de Lume salt crater has salt pans set inside the crater of an extinct volcano; the brine is so dense that you float without effort. The same half-day island tour usually takes in the Buracona blue eye, a sunlit rock pool on the west coast, and the shimmering flats of Terra Boa.

On Boa Vista, desert and dune tours can explore the Viana desert, the dunes protected in the Morro de Areia nature reserve, and the north coast to the rusting hull of the Cabo Santa Maria shipwreck.

Walk through history on Santiago

Santiago is where Cape Verde's story begins. Cidade Velha, settled in 1462 as Ribeira Grande, was the first settlement on the islands and became the country's first UNESCO World Heritage site in 2009. Walk its old streets, then climb to the Fort Real de São Filipe for the view over the town and bay.

In the capital, Praia, the old town on the Platô has the markets, squares and government buildings. In the north, near Tarrafal, the Tarrafal camp museum occupies the former prison camp where Portugal's dictatorship held political prisoners; it began operating on 29 October 1936 and, after a break, held its last prisoners until 1 May 1974. It is a sobering, important visit. Between the two, the Serra Malagueta Natural Park offers green hill walks.

Hear live music in Mindelo

Music is the country's best-known export, and Mindelo on São Vicente is its home town. Morna, the slow, aching song form that Cesária Évora carried around the world, was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2019. Evenings in Mindelo's old town are the easiest place to hear it live; see live music and morna.

Time a trip for a festival if you can. The Mindelo carnival is associated with Carnival Tuesday, which falls on 9 February in 2027; this calendar date does not confirm a 2027 parade programme. In August the Baía das Gatas festival fills the beach of the same name. On Santiago, the Atlantic Music Expo has published dates of 5 to 8 April 2027 in Praia, and it runs just before the Kriol Jazz Festival. See all Cape Verde events.

Hike the valleys of Santo Antão

Santo Antão is the walker's island, a block of mountains split by deep green valleys and terraced fields. The Paul valley is the best known, with sugar cane, villages and paths down to the sea, and the village of Fontainhas clings to a ridge above a terraced ravine. Much of the best walking lies inside the Cova, Paul and Ribeira da Torre Natural Park.

The island has no operating airport (a new one is planned at Porto Novo), so you arrive by ferry from Mindelo. Plan routes with hiking in Santo Antão, and use the 7-day São Vicente and Santo Antão hiking itinerary to combine walking days with nights in Mindelo.

Climb the volcano on Fogo

Fogo is a single volcano rising out of the sea. Its summit, Pico do Fogo, reaches about 2,829 metres, the highest point in Cape Verde. Below it lies Chã das Caldeiras, a plain inside the old crater where people live and grow grapes, and where an eruption that began on 23 November 2014 destroyed much of the village of Portela. The uplands include Fogo Natural Park.

Climbing Pico do Fogo is a steep, loose scramble that takes most of a day; go with a local guide, start early and carry plenty of water. Reach Fogo via Santiago; the Santiago and Fogo 7-day itinerary shows how. The UK government notes that sea travel to Fogo and Brava is often disrupted, so leave slack in your plans.

Eat cachupa and taste grogue

Cape Verdean food is hearty and built on corn, beans and fish. Cachupa, a slow-cooked stew of corn and beans with vegetables and often meat or fish, is the national dish; the next morning, leftovers are fried into cachupa refogada. Look for grilled lobster, caldo de peixe fish soup, pastel com diabo dentro (pastries with a spicy filling) and goat's cheese served with papaya jam.

Grogue is a local sugar-cane spirit. Sweeter ponche, is made with grogue. Browse Cape Verdean dishes for more.

Fitting it together

  • One week, one island: beaches, wind sports and an island tour on Sal or Boa Vista. Read things to do in Sal or things to do in Boa Vista.
  • One week, two linked islands: São Vicente with Santo Antão, or Santiago with Fogo.
  • Ten days or more: a beach island plus one of those pairs, joined by a domestic flight. See the island-hopping guide.

Not sure where to base yourself? Which Cape Verde island is best compares them all, and the best time to visit explains the wind and the short wet season.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Cape Verde best known for?

Long white beaches and steady wind on Sal and Boa Vista, morna music and Cesária Évora, the Fogo volcano, hiking on Santo Antão, and Cidade Velha, the country's UNESCO World Heritage site on Santiago.

Is there more to do in Cape Verde than the beach?

Yes, but much of it is on other islands. Santiago has the history, São Vicente the music, Santo Antão the hiking and Fogo the volcano. From Sal or Boa Vista, the main non-beach activities are island tours, desert trips, turtle and whale watching and water sports.

When can you see turtles and whales in Cape Verde?

Loggerhead turtles nest from June to October, with hatchlings from August into December. Humpback whales breed from February to May, especially off Boa Vista. Watch turtles only on a certified guided tour within the authorised observation window.

Can you climb Pico do Fogo without a guide?

The climb is steep, loose and long, and the tourism institute says the trail must be accompanied by a local mountain guide. Start early, carry plenty of water and check conditions in Chã das Caldeiras the day before.

What should I eat and drink in Cape Verde?

Try cachupa, the national corn and bean stew, and its fried breakfast version, cachupa refogada, plus grilled fish and lobster and goat's cheese with papaya jam. To drink, taste grogue, the local sugar-cane spirit, or the sweeter ponche.

guides.title: Things to Do in Sal, Cape Verde: A Guide by Interest
guides.summary: Sal is a beach, wind and water island. This guide sorts its sights by interest, gives the official turtle and whale watching rules, and says plainly what to skip.
guides.html:
Sal is a beach-holiday island in Cape Verde. It is flat, dry and windy, with a resort base around the town of Santa Maria on the south coast and its international airport, Amílcar Cabral International (SID), in the middle of the island. The country's official name is Cabo Verde, and Sal is one of its ten islands. What follows is organised by interest, so you can skip straight to what you came for, and it ends with an honest note on what Sal is not good for.

Beaches and swimming

The long sweep of Santa Maria beach is the reason most people book Sal. It runs in front of the town and the hotel strip, with pale sand and turquoise water, and it is the easiest place on the island to spend a lazy day. West of town, Ponta Preta is wilder and better known for waves than for paddling. At the island's southern tip, Ponta Sino is a walk from the hotels for a different angle on the coast, and over on the east side Kite Beach belongs to the wind sports crowd.

Take the sea seriously. The UK government's travel advice says tides and currents around the islands are very strong, that waves can have a strong undertow, and that you should always use beaches where a lifeguard is on duty. It also explains the flag system: red means do not go in, yellow means you can walk in the water but not swim, and green means it is safe to swim. Ask at your hotel which stretches are supervised, and treat the empty beaches away from Santa Maria as places to look at rather than swim.

Wind, waves and water sports

The same trade winds that keep Sal feeling fresh make it one of the best-known wind sports spots in the Atlantic. Kitesurfing centres on Kite Beach and the bays around Santa Maria, where schools teach beginners and rent kit to experienced riders. Windsurfing has a long history here too, and Santa Maria's bay is the usual base. For surfing, Ponta Preta is the name to know: its waves call for experience, so beginners should book a lesson where an instructor chooses the beach.

If you are not a kiter, the wind still matters. It can make a beach day feel cooler than the forecast suggests, and it blows sand around on exposed stretches. Our guide to Cape Verde in winter covers what that means between November and March.

Diving and snorkelling

Sal is a good place to learn to dive or to add easy boat dives to a beach holiday. Scuba diving centres operate from Santa Maria, with reef and wreck sites within a short boat ride. Ask your dive operator about its licence, instructor credentials, certification checks and medical screening before you book.

Snorkelling works best on calm mornings from sheltered spots near Santa Maria, or on a boat trip. On the west coast, the Baía da Murdeira is a designated marine nature reserve within the country's national network of protected areas. Ask your operator about the reserve rules before entering the water. Wind and swell decide everything: if your operator says the water is too rough, believe them.

Wildlife: sharks, turtles and whales

Lemon sharks at Shark Bay

Shark Bay is the trip almost every Sal visitor hears about: you wade in shallow water while young lemon sharks circle nearby. Project Biodiversity, the Sal-based conservation charity, monitors a juvenile lemon shark nursery at Parda Reef in the north-east of the island and reports that lemon sharks are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN, yet remain unprotected under Cape Verdean law. Follow the charity's wildlife guidance. The charity's responsible tourism guidelines ask visitors never to feed wildlife and to choose government-certified operators and guides. Wear reef shoes for the rocks, keep still, and never touch or chase the sharks.

Turtle watching

Sal is one of the main nesting islands for loggerhead turtles, and night walks to watch a female lay her eggs are popular in summer. They are regulated. Project Biodiversity's turtle season page gives the official observation dates for 2026, as of November 2026, as 1 July until the end of September, excluding specific nesting beaches. Those dates concern 2026; confirm the authorised dates and beaches for a future trip. Winter is outside the nesting-tour window.

The national turtle watching regulation (Decreto-lei n.º 50/2024) sets the rules on the beach. Visitors may only use red-light torches, with white light and flash photography expressly banned. A group of no more than ten visitors approaches each turtle, in a line behind the nature guide, and visitors may never be left alone on the beach. Book turtle watching only with a guided excursion, never on your own.

Whales

Humpback whales use Cape Verde's waters to breed. A good-practice guide for nature excursions, validated by the national environment and tourism directorates, says two populations use the islands: the North Atlantic one from February to May and a Southern Hemisphere one from July to October. The same guide sets a watching zone of no less than 60 metres from the animals, rising to 100 metres when calves are present. Boa Vista is the island most associated with whale watching, but boat trips run from Sal too, so ask your operator how it follows those distances.

Salt, blue water and mirages: the island tour

Sal's inland sights are usually done in one half-day or full-day island tour by 4x4 or minibus, and the three below are the core of it.

  • Pedra de Lume salt crater: old salt pans inside a volcanic crater on the east coast, where you can float in the dense brine. The area is designated the Salinas de Pedra de Lume e Cagarral Protected Landscape. Rinse off afterwards and keep the salty water away from your eyes.
  • Buracona and the Blue Eye: a rocky inlet on the north-west coast where a pool in the lava lights up blue when the sun is overhead. It sits inside the Buracona-Ragona Protected Landscape. The effect depends on direct sunlight, so a hazy or cloudy day can disappoint, and the rocks are no place for a swim when the sea is up.
  • Terra Boa: a flat plain near Espargos where the heat haze produces mirages that look like water. The mirage depends on the conditions.

Tours often add the fishing village of Palmeira and the capital, Espargos. If you want the island as a whole in a few days, our Sal 5-day itinerary and Sal 7-day itinerary slot these in around beach time.

Santa Maria town: pier, food and music

The Santa Maria pier is the town's landmark. A storm partly destroyed it in October 2024 and it is being rebuilt, with completion reported for October 2027, so expect works and restricted access and ask locally what is open. Walk the streets behind the seafront for small bars and restaurants away from the hotel buffets.

Food is worth an evening of its own. Try cachupa, the national stew of hominy, beans and whatever the cook adds, and the fried breakfast version, cachupa refogada. Seafood is the obvious order on the coast: grilled lobster where it is on the menu, búzio (sea snail) and caldo de peixe, the fish broth. Finish with grogue, the sugar cane spirit, or the sweeter ponche.

Evenings in Santa Maria often come with live music. Many bars and restaurants host musicians playing morna and coladeira, and our live music and morna page explains what you are hearing. If your dates line up, the Santa Maria festival is the town's big annual party. Anglers can book sport fishing trips from the town too.

What Sal is not good for

Sal is excellent at what it does and weak at a lot of other things. Knowing that before you book saves disappointment.

  • Hiking and green scenery. The island is predominantly flat and arid. For mountain trails, terraced valleys and cool air, go to Santo Antão and read about hiking in Santo Antão, or climb a volcano on Fogo.
  • History and culture. Sal has little old architecture. The country's colonial history is on Santiago, at the UNESCO-listed Cidade Velha, and its music culture is strongest in Mindelo.
  • Still, calm beach days in winter. The wind that kiters love can make the beach breezy and the sea choppy. If you want flat water every day, Sal in the windy months is not the place.
  • Swimming anywhere you like. Many beaches have strong currents and no lifeguard. Stick to supervised water.
  • Getting under the skin of Cape Verde on a short stay. Santa Maria is built around tourism. If daily life matters to you, add a second island using our island hopping guide.

Still deciding between the two resort islands? Our Sal or Boa Vista comparison and which Cape Verde island is best guide lay out the trade-offs.

Practical notes

  • Getting around: the UK government advises using only authorised taxis from ranks or called by your hotel, and says that on Sal and Boa Vista authorised taxis are blue and yellow. Agree the fare before you set off.
  • Safety: the same advice notes that crime is generally low but can include pickpocketing, bag snatching and muggings, particularly in Praia and on Sal and Boa Vista. Our guide to whether Cape Verde is safe has the detail, and emergency contacts lists the numbers.
  • Weather: UK advice gives the rainy season as mid-August to mid-October and warns that dust haze (bruma seca) can occur between December and February. See the best time to visit Cape Verde and the weather page.
  • Before you fly: check the pre-arrival registration and airport fee on our visa and entry requirements guide, and how to pay for things in currency and money.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days do you need on Sal?

Three or four days cover the island tour, Shark Bay, a boat trip and plenty of beach time. A week suits people who want to learn to kitesurf or dive, or who simply want a long rest on Santa Maria beach. If you have more time than that, add a second island rather than more days on Sal.

Can you see turtles on Sal in winter?

Winter is outside the nesting-tour season. As of November 2026, Project Biodiversity gives the official observation dates for 2026, as of November 2026, as 1 July until the end of September, excluding specific nesting beaches. Confirm the authorised dates for a future trip. Outside the season, the charity's visitor programme and education work are the way to learn about Sal's loggerheads.

Is it safe to swim at Santa Maria beach?

Swim where a lifeguard is on duty and follow the flags. UK travel advice warns that tides and currents around the islands are very strong and that a red flag means do not go into the water, while yellow means you can walk in but not swim.

Is Shark Bay on Sal worth doing?

It can be a memorable visit if you go with a guide who keeps the group calm and does not feed the sharks. Project Biodiversity reports that lemon sharks remain unprotected under Cape Verdean law; choose an operator who follows its wildlife guidance.

Is Sal good for families?

Yes, for a beach-based holiday with a pool and short excursions. Keep children in supervised water, plan around the wind on exposed beaches, and do not expect green parks or much natural shade outside hotel grounds.

guides.title: Which Cape Verde Island Is Best? An Honest Island-by-Island Comparison
guides.summary: Sal and Boa Vista for beaches and easy flights, Santo Antão for hiking, São Vicente for music, Santiago for history, Fogo for the volcano: a fair comparison table and realistic combinations.
guides.html:
Cape Verde (officially Cabo Verde) is not one destination but nine inhabited islands, and the gap between them is wide. Sal and Boa Vista are flat, sandy and windy, built around resort holidays. Santo Antão is a wall of green ravines with no beach life to speak of. Fogo is a single volcano. Mindelo on São Vicente is a port town that runs on music. Picking the wrong island for what you want is the most common way to come home disappointed, so this guide compares them honestly and then suggests combinations that work on the ground.

A quick piece of geography explains most of the differences. Sal, Boa Vista and Maio are low, level and dry, with long sandy beaches. Santiago, Fogo, Santo Antão and São Nicolau are mountainous, with upland valleys and walking trails. If you want sand, look east. If you want mountains, look west and south.

The islands compared at a glance

The table gives editorial ratings for beaches, wind exposure, walking, culture and quiet, rather than measured rankings. Flight access is described in general terms for travellers from the UK and Ireland, because routes change every season; always check current schedules before you book.

Brava, the smallest inhabited island, is left out of the table because reaching it depends on the ferry from Fogo, which the UK government notes is often disrupted. It suits travellers with time to spare and flexible plans.

Sal: a beach-holiday base

Sal is a popular beach-holiday base. Sal airport handled about 1.58 million passengers in 2025 according to its operator, and the drive to Santa Maria at the southern tip is short. Santa Maria beach faces south, away from the prevailing north-east wind, but wind shelter does not establish safe swimming conditions. The town has restaurants, bars and the Santa Maria pier; check the location of your hotel.

Sal is also the kitesurfing island. Kite Beach on the east coast and Ponta Preta draw riders through the windy months, and kitesurfing and windsurfing schools cater to beginners. Inland, the island is flat and brown, but it has three easy half-day trips: the Pedra de Lume salt crater, where salt pans fill an old volcanic crater and you can float in the brine; the Buracona blue eye pool on the west coast; and Shark Bay, where juvenile lemon sharks use the shallows as a nursery all year.

Pick Sal if you want a straightforward winter-sun week with plenty of flight options, a walkable resort town and wind sports. Skip it if you want greenery, hiking or a sense of traditional island life.

Boa Vista: bigger beaches, more space

Boa Vista looks like a piece of the Sahara dropped into the Atlantic. For broad beaches, consider Praia de Santa Mónica and Praia de Chaves, which run for kilometres. Check current flights and the transfer to the main town, Sal Rei. Many visitors stay in large all-inclusive resorts spread along the coast, so check how far yours is from town before you book if you want to wander out to eat.

Boa Vista is the island for wildlife. It is an important loggerhead turtle nesting island. Turtle watching requires certified guides and authorised observation dates, which are shorter than the June to October nesting season. As of November 2026, Project Biodiversity gives 1 July to the end of September for 2026, excluding specific nesting beaches; confirm future dates before booking. From roughly February to May, humpback whales gather to breed off the island, and researchers have described the bay of Sal Rei as the single most important winter breeding bay for the species in the eastern North Atlantic; see whale watching. The Viana desert and the Cabo Santa Maria shipwreck are the classic desert and dune tour stops.

Pick Boa Vista if you want huge empty beaches, an all-inclusive base, turtles or whales. Skip it if you want a lively town on your doorstep or easy access to other islands.

Santiago: history, the capital and a real African city

Santiago is the largest island and the most Cape Verdean in feel. Praia, the capital, has a compact old town on the Platô, markets and the April music events. A short drive west along the coast, Cidade Velha, founded by the Portuguese in the fifteenth century, became the country's first UNESCO World Heritage site in 2009; the Fort Real de São Filipe looks down on it. In the north, Tarrafal has a calm bay beach and the Tarrafal camp museum, the former prison camp opened under Portugal's dictatorship in 1936. The Serra Malagueta Natural Park gives the island proper hill walking.

Pick Santiago if you care about history, food and everyday life more than resort comfort. It pairs naturally with Fogo.

São Vicente and Santo Antão: music and mountains

Mindelo, the port town of São Vicente, is the cultural centre of the country. Morna, the slow song form made famous by Cesária Évora, was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in 2019, and evenings in Mindelo are the easiest place to hear it; see live music and morna. Mindelo's old town is walkable and the Mindelo carnival is a major annual event. Beaches here are modest: Laginha is the town beach, with São Pedro and Baía das Gatas further out.

Across the channel, Santo Antão is the hiking island, with terraced valleys, cliff paths and villages reached on foot. The Paul valley and the cliff-side village of Fontainhas are the famous names; see hiking in Santo Antão. There is no operating airport (a new one is planned at Porto Novo), so you arrive by ferry from Mindelo.

Pick this pair if you want culture by night and serious walking by day. It is the best two-island combination in Cape Verde.

Fogo: the volcano

Fogo rises to Pico do Fogo, at about 2,829 metres the highest point in the country. Inside the old crater, the plain of Chã das Caldeiras holds villages rebuilt after the eruption that began on 23 November 2014 and buried much of them in lava. Climbing Pico do Fogo is a steep, loose, full-day effort; the tourism institute says the trail must be accompanied by a local mountain guide. The town of São Filipe is colonial and handsome, and the Bandeira de São Filipe festival peaks around 1 May. The uplands include Fogo Natural Park.

Pick Fogo if you want one extraordinary landscape and do not mind basic lodging. Reach it via Santiago.

Maio and São Nicolau: for real quiet

Maio has the sand of Sal with a fraction of the visitors; Bitxe Rotxa beach near Vila do Maio is typical. São Nicolau is mountainous, green in places and very little visited. Both need a domestic flight or a ferry, and both reward travellers who are happy with simple guesthouses and slow days.

Best island for...

  • A first winter-sun week: Sal, for flight choice and a walkable resort town.
  • Families wanting space and an all-inclusive: Boa Vista, choosing a resort with a sheltered swimming area or a pool.
  • Kitesurfing and windsurfing: Sal first, then Boa Vista.
  • Turtles and whales: Boa Vista (turtle tours on authorised summer dates, whales roughly February to May).
  • Hiking: Santo Antão, with Fogo for a single big summit.
  • Music and nightlife with local character: Mindelo on São Vicente.
  • History: Santiago, for Cidade Velha and Tarrafal.
  • Getting away from everyone: Maio or São Nicolau.

Combinations that work

Inter-island travel is the part that catches people out. Check current domestic flight routes directly with the airline and ferry sailings with the operator. The UK government warns that sea conditions can be dangerous and that travel to Fogo and Brava can often be disrupted. Build in a spare day and read the island hopping page and the island-hopping guide before you commit.

  • São Vicente and Santo Antão (7 days or more): a practical pairing, subject to the current ferry timetable and sea conditions. See the 7-day hiking itinerary.
  • Santiago and Fogo (7 days or more): history plus the volcano. See the Santiago and Fogo itinerary.
  • Sal plus São Vicente (10 days or more): beach first, then culture, subject to a suitable domestic flight being available.
  • Sal and Boa Vista: possible but awkward in one week; the Sal or Boa Vista guide explains why.

If you only have a week and want a beach, stay on one island. Our Sal 7-day itinerary and Boa Vista 5-day itinerary show how to fill the time, and the best time to visit covers the wind and the short wet season.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which Cape Verde island is best for a first visit?

For most first-time visitors from the UK and Ireland, Sal. Check direct flights for your dates; Santa Maria offers a resort-town base and a south-facing beach. If you would rather have more space and a quieter all-inclusive, choose Boa Vista.

Which Cape Verde island has the best beaches?

Sal and Boa Vista offer white-sand beaches, with Maio a quieter alternative. Beach conditions vary; Santa Maria is a convenient town base. Currents around the islands can be strong, so swim only where a lifeguard is on duty.

Which island is best for hiking?

Santo Antão, reached by ferry from Mindelo on São Vicente. Fogo offers the demanding climb of Pico do Fogo, and Santiago has good trails in the Serra Malagueta Natural Park.

Can I visit two islands in one week?

Consider São Vicente with Santo Antão, or Santiago with Fogo, if the current transport schedules leave enough contingency time. Pairs that depend on infrequent sailings or flights, such as Sal and Boa Vista, are harder. Leave a buffer day before your flight home.

Which island is the least windy?

Exposure varies by coast and valley. Ask about conditions at the specific beach or walking route; a whole-island wind ranking cannot predict the day's weather.

destinations.name: Boa Vista
destinations.tagline: Big, empty island of dunes, long beaches and nesting turtles
destinations.summary: Boa Vista is Cape Verde's dune island: long, empty beaches, the Viana desert, nesting loggerhead turtles in summer and a handful of large resorts, with Sal Rei as its small capital.
destinations.html:
Boa Vista is the easternmost island of Cape Verde and, at about 620 square kilometres, almost three times the size of Sal. Like Sal it is low and dry: the highest point, Monte Estância, is 390 metres. What sets it apart is space. Long beaches run for kilometres without buildings, sand dunes drift inland, and outside the capital Sal Rei and a few villages, the island is largely empty.

Tourism here is concentrated in a few large all-inclusive resorts, mostly on the west and south coasts, and many guests rarely leave them. Those who do find the Viana desert, a field of pale dunes that the tourism institute calls the largest desert in the archipelago, and the rusting Cabo Santa Maria shipwreck on the north coast. Praia de Santa Mónica in the southwest runs for more than 11 kilometres.

What to do on Boa Vista

  • Walk the sand at Praia de Chaves, Santa Mónica and Varandinha.
  • Join a desert and dune tour to the Viana desert and the Morro de Areia nature reserve.
  • See loggerhead turtles nesting on a licensed turtle-watching walk in the summer season.
  • Visit the Cabo Santa Maria wreck; Ponta Sino is on Sal and requires a separate island visit.
  • Look for whales on a whale-watching trip; check seasonal availability before booking.

How Boa Vista differs from Sal

Both islands are arid, windy and built for beach holidays. Sal has a real resort town in Santa Maria, with bars and restaurants you can walk between; Boa Vista's resorts are more spread out and isolated, and Sal Rei is a quiet local town rather than a nightlife strip. Boa Vista wins on emptiness, dunes and turtles. Boa Vista has loggerhead nesting beaches, and the national turtle network's manual gives the season as running generally from 1 June to 31 October. Our Sal or Boa Vista guide compares the two in detail.

Neither island is the place for green hiking country or historic towns: for those, look at Santo Antão, Santiago or Mindelo. The UK government lists Boa Vista among the places where pickpocketing, bag snatching and muggings occur, and says medical facilities are particularly limited on the island. International flights land at Aristides Pereira International Airport, reached by road from Sal Rei. For a plan, see the Boa Vista 5-day itinerary and things to do in Boa Vista.

destinations.name: Fogo
destinations.tagline: Volcano island: the 2,829 m Pico do Fogo, crater villages and wine
destinations.summary: Fogo is Cape Verde's volcano island: the 2,829-metre Pico do Fogo, the lava-filled crater of Chã das Caldeiras, volcanic wine and the old town of São Filipe. Best for hikers.
destinations.html:
Fogo is a single volcano rising out of the Atlantic in the southwest of Cape Verde. The island covers about 476 square kilometres and has around 35,000 people, according to the tourism institute, and its summit, Pico do Fogo, stands at about 2,829 metres, the highest point in the country. The volcano is active: in 2014 lava swallowed villages and farmland in the crater, and the Canadian government notes that it remains at risk of future eruptions.

Inside the old crater lies Chã das Caldeiras, a high plain ringed by lava walls where people still farm vines and fruit in black volcanic soil. The area is protected as the Fogo Natural Park. The island's capital, São Filipe, sits on the west coast, and much of its architecture dates from the colonial period.

What to do on Fogo

  • Climb Pico do Fogo with a local mountain guide; read our climbing guide first.
  • Stay a night in Chã das Caldeiras to walk the crater floor at dawn.
  • Taste Fogo wine, made as red, white and rosé from vines grown on volcanic soil.
  • Walk the old streets of São Filipe and see the Bandeira de São Filipe festival around 1 May.

Practical notes

The tourism institute says the hike into the heart of the crater can take up to six hours and should be done with a local mountain guide. The summit climb is steep, loose and exposed, and only for fit walkers. Earth tremors are felt occasionally on Fogo and Brava, according to the UK government, which also reports that Cape Verde raised its dengue warning level on Santiago, Fogo and Brava. Follow local authority instructions on any volcanic activity.

Getting here takes planning. Fogo has a domestic aerodrome at São Filipe, and ferries sail from Praia on Santiago, but the UK government warns that sea travel to Fogo and Brava is often disrupted. Build in spare days and read our island-hopping guide. The Santiago and Fogo 7-day itinerary pairs the two islands.

destinations.name: Maio
destinations.tagline: Quiet, flat island of empty beaches, salt pans and nesting turtles
destinations.summary: Maio is the quiet beach island near Santiago: long empty sands, old salt pans at Vila do Maio, an acacia forest, nesting turtles in summer and very little development.
destinations.html:
Maio is a low, dry island a short hop east of Santiago, covering a little under 270 square kilometres with a population of several thousand. The highest point, Monte Penoso, is about 500 metres. Like Sal and Boa Vista it has long pale beaches, but it has almost none of their resort building. Visitors who come here want empty sand, small villages and a slow pace.

The capital, Vila do Maio, was once known as Porto Inglês, after the British ships that loaded salt here, and the salt pans beside the town remain part of its identity. The town beach, Bitxe Rotxa, is close to the centre. Inland at Calheta, acacia trees form what the tourism institute calls the largest managed forest area in Cape Verde.

What to do on Maio

  • Swim and walk at Bitxe Rotxa and the other beaches around the coast.
  • See the salt pans next to Vila do Maio.
  • Join a guided turtle-watching walk in the nesting season.
  • Cycle between villages: the tourism institute calls cycling an interesting way to explore.

Maio is an important nesting island for loggerhead turtles. The Maio Biodiversity Foundation gives the nesting season as June to October and recommends visits with trained local guides. As of November 2026, use no white lights or flash, keep your distance and follow the guide's instructions.

Facilities are limited, with guesthouses and small hotels rather than resorts, and cars with drivers and rentals available in Vila do Maio. Maio has a domestic aerodrome, and ferries run from Praia, but check schedules close to travel in our island-hopping guide. The UK government warns that sea conditions around Cape Verde can be dangerous and advises swimming only where a lifeguard is on duty; check that a lifeguard is on duty before entering the water.

destinations.name: Mindelo and São Vicente
destinations.tagline: Port city of music, colonial streets and the ferry to Santo Antão
destinations.summary: Mindelo is the port capital of São Vicente and Cape Verde's cultural city: colonial streets, live morna, the February or March carnival, nearby beaches and the ferry to Santo Antão.
destinations.html:
Mindelo is the capital and main city of São Vicente, a small, dry island of about 227 square kilometres and roughly 80,000 people, according to the tourism institute. The city wraps around the deep natural harbour of Porto Grande, and its pastel colonial buildings, squares and waterfront give it the strongest sense of place of any town in Cape Verde. It is the country's music and carnival city, and the home island of the singer Cesária Évora.

Most visitors base themselves in the old town, a walkable grid of streets around the municipal market, the fish market and the waterfront. Evenings are the time for live morna and coladeira in bars and restaurants. The island's highest point, Monte Verde, rises to 774 metres and is protected as the Monte Verde Natural Park.

What to do in Mindelo and on São Vicente

  • Walk the old town and markets, and see our page on the Cesária Évora museum.
  • Swim at Laginha, the city beach, or drive to São Pedro and Baía das Gatas.
  • Join the Mindelo Carnival in February or March, or the Baía das Gatas Festival in August.
  • Drive or hike up to Monte Verde for views over the island.
  • Take the ferry to Santo Antão for a day or several days of hiking.

Mindelo is the natural partner to Santo Antão, which has no working airport: check the ferry operator's timetable for your travel date. Many visitors fly into São Vicente airport, near São Pedro, then spend a few nights in Mindelo before and after the hiking. See the São Vicente and Santo Antão 7-day hiking itinerary.

São Vicente is as arid as Sal, and its beaches are fewer and smaller than those on the resort islands. Come for the city, the music and the food rather than a week on the sand. The Canadian government notes that theft is common at outdoor markets on São Vicente, including in Mindelo, so keep bags closed and phones out of reach in crowds, especially during carnival.

destinations.name: Praia
destinations.tagline: Cape Verde capital on Santiago: Platô old town, markets and music
destinations.summary: Praia is the capital of Cape Verde, on the south coast of Santiago: the Platô old town, busy markets, city beaches, live music and the base for Cidade Velha and the interior.
destinations.html:
Praia is the capital of Cape Verde (officially Cabo Verde) and its most populous city, set on the south coast of Santiago. It is a working city of government offices, markets and neighbourhoods spread across flat-topped plateaus and the valleys between them, and it feels nothing like the resort towns of Sal or Boa Vista. Visitors come for history, food, music and as a base for exploring the island.

The historic core is the Platô, a raised old town of colonial-era streets, a central square and the main church, with views over the harbour. Below it, the city spreads into surrounding neighbourhoods. Small beaches sit between the headlands, including Quebra Canela, a city beach popular with local families at weekends.

What to do in Praia

  • Walk the Platô old town, its square and the market streets.
  • Take a half-day trip to UNESCO-listed Cidade Velha and the Fort Real de São Filipe, about 15 kilometres west.
  • Swim at Quebra Canela or drive to São Francisco Beach east of the city.
  • Hear live music in the city's bars and cultural venues.
  • Plan around the Kriol Jazz Festival, the Atlantic Music Expo and the Gamboa Festival.

Praia is the main gateway for the southern islands. Nelson Mandela International Airport lies about 3 kilometres northeast of the centre, and the harbour is the departure point for ferries to Fogo and Maio. The UK government warns that sea travel to Fogo and Brava is often disrupted, so read our island-hopping guide and keep a spare day in your plans.

Take ordinary city precautions. The UK government names Praia as a place where pickpocketing, bag snatching and muggings occur, and the Canadian government says crime is higher on Santiago, especially in Praia. Use registered taxis after dark, keep phones out of sight in busy areas and leave valuables in your hotel. The emergency contacts page lists the police, ambulance and fire numbers.

destinations.name: Sal
destinations.tagline: Flat, dry and windy island of long beaches, salt pans and kite spots
destinations.summary: Sal is Cape Verde's main beach-holiday island: flat desert land, steady trade winds, the long white beach at Santa Maria, the Pedra de Lume salt crater and the country's largest airport.
destinations.html:
Sal is a popular island for beach holidays in Cape Verde. It sits in the northeast of the archipelago, covers about 215 square kilometres and is almost entirely flat: the highest point, Monte Grande, reaches only 406 metres. The island is mostly dry. The land is stony desert and salt flat, the wind blows hard for much of the year, and the reason to come is the sea, the sun and the beach at Santa Maria in the far south.

Resorts are a major part of tourism on Sal. Large all-inclusive hotels line the coast either side of Santa Maria, and international flights arrive at Amílcar Cabral International Airport, which the airport operator describes as the largest airport infrastructure in the country. The island's administrative capital is Espargos, a working town near the airport, and the small port of Palmeira on the west coast handles fishing boats and cargo.

What to do on Sal

  • Spend beach days on Santa Maria Beach and Ponta Preta, the island's best-known sand.
  • Float in the brine of the Pedra de Lume salt crater, where salt has been worked since the early 1800s.
  • Watch the light in the rock pool at Buracona on the northwest coast.
  • Wade among young lemon sharks at Shark Bay and see the mirage plain of Terra Boa.
  • Learn or ride at Kite Beach on the windy east coast, or book kitesurfing, windsurfing and scuba diving.

Who Sal suits, and who it does not

Sal is a strong choice for a week of reliable winter sun, an easy direct flight and a resort pool, and for wind and water sports. It is a weak choice if you want hiking, dramatic scenery or a sense of Cape Verdean town life. For mountain walking go to Santo Antão; for history and culture, Santiago and Mindelo on São Vicente. Neighbouring Boa Vista is the closest comparison: also arid and resort-based, but larger, emptier and with bigger dunes. Our guide to Sal or Boa Vista sets the two side by side.

The UK government lists Sal, with Boa Vista and Praia, as places where pickpocketing, bag snatching and muggings can occur, so keep valuables in the hotel safe and take care on quiet streets at night. Its advice for swimmers is to use beaches with a lifeguard on duty, because currents around the islands are very strong. For a ready-made plan, see the 5-day and 7-day Sal itineraries and our list of things to do in Sal.

photo.alt: Santa Maria beach and seafront hotel on the island of Sal

destinations.name: Sal Rei
destinations.tagline: Boa Vista capital: a quiet town square, harbour and long town beach
destinations.summary: Sal Rei is the small capital of Boa Vista: a central square, a fishing harbour, the long Praia de Estoril beach and the base for boat trips, dune tours and local restaurants.
destinations.html:
Sal Rei is the capital of Boa Vista, set on the west coast and reached by road from Boa Vista airport. The tourism institute notes that the name comes from salt, an important product in the 18th century. Today it is a quiet, low-rise place of painted houses around a central square and church, with a small harbour where fishing boats come and go.

The town is the practical heart of Boa Vista for anyone staying outside a resort. Guesthouses, small hotels, restaurants and tour desks are here, along with local shops. South of the harbour, Praia de Estoril is a long town beach popular for kitesurfing and windsurfing.

What to do in Sal Rei

  • Swim, kite or windsurf at Praia de Estoril beside the town.
  • Book kitesurfing, diving and whale-watching trips that leave from the harbour.
  • Head inland on a dune tour to the Viana desert, which starts close to town.
  • Drive north to the Cabo Santa Maria wreck and Praia da Varandinha further south.
  • Eat grilled fish and cachupa in the local restaurants around the square.

Sal Rei suits independent travellers, kitesurfers and anyone who prefers a town base to an all-inclusive resort. It is quiet at night compared with Santa Maria on Sal, and the island beyond it is large and thinly served by public transport, so most visitors rely on taxis, organised tours or a rented 4x4 to reach the beaches and dunes.

The UK government lists Boa Vista among places where pickpocketing, bag snatching and muggings can occur, and notes that medical facilities on the island are particularly limited, so carry good travel insurance. It also advises swimming only where a lifeguard is on duty. During the summer nesting season, follow the rules of licensed guides on any beach where loggerhead turtles lay eggs, and book turtle watching through a licensed operator.
